opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting question, and I think there's a pretty natural argument that, in equilibrium, you'd expect spending on training and inference to be roughly comparable, within the same order of magnitude.

The intuition is that there's a tradeoff between the two. You can get a given level of capability by training a bigger model for longer, or by taking a smaller model and spending more compute at inference time: sampling many times and picking the best answer, longer chains of reasoning, search, verification, that kind of thing. If you're a developer trying to minimize the total cost of delivering some level of performance, you'll push on whichever margin is cheaper until the marginal returns roughly equalize. In a lot of reasonable models of that tradeoff, the optimum lands with similar amounts spent on each side.

There's also a deployment angle. As models become more economically valuable, the number of people and tasks using them grows a lot, so the total inference bill can get very large. That pushes labs to train models longer than would be "compute-optimal" in the narrow Chinchilla sense. You overtrain a smaller model because it's cheaper to serve at scale. So scaling up usage shifts some of the burden back into training, in a way that makes the two kinds of spending track each other.

What I think changes as we scale is the character of inference. Historically, inference was mostly a single forward pass per token, fairly cheap per query. Now, with reasoning models and agents running for long horizons, inference compute per task can be enormous. That opens up a much bigger lever on the inference side, and I'd expect it to grow substantially as a share of total compute, at least for a while.

One implication I find important is that once you've trained a model, the inference compute you have determines how many copies you can run and how much thinking each copy can do. If training and inference spending are comparable, then whoever trained a frontier model already has a huge amount of compute to deploy it. That has real consequences for how quickly AI capabilities could translate into economic impact, or into automating AI research itself, once systems cross certain capability thresholds.

r001.rationale: The response describes a trade-off and says marginal returns should equalize, but it does not clearly state that the appropriate spending ratio depends on the slope of the performance trade-off.

r002.rationale: It says that as models scale, inference shifts toward reasoning and long-running agents, opening a much bigger lever for inference compute and potentially increasing its share of total compute.

r003.rationale: It says developers push on whichever margin is cheaper until marginal returns equalize, communicating that increasing the lower-return-cost budget can capture available gains.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we've thought about quite a bit at Epoch. There's a nice way to frame it, which is that training compute and inference compute are, to some extent, substitutes for each other. You can spend more during training to get a model that's more capable per token of inference, or you can take a smaller model and spend more at inference time, through things like chain-of-thought, sampling many times, searching over outputs, and get to a similar level of performance. So there's a kind of trade-off frontier.

Now, what determines where you sit on that frontier? It's basically how much the model is going to be used. Training is a fixed cost that you pay once, and inference is a cost you pay every time the model is used. So if you expect to serve a model to hundreds of millions of users, it makes sense to over-train it, to spend a lot more on training than the Chinchilla-optimal recipe would suggest, because every bit of efficiency you squeeze out at inference time gets multiplied across an enormous number of queries. That's roughly what we've seen with models like Llama, where they train on far more tokens than would be optimal if you only cared about the training budget.

The flip side is that as you scale up training, the absolute inference cost per query also tends to go up, because the models get bigger. So the total compute budget of these labs is shifting. A few years ago, I'd guess the majority of compute went to training frontier runs. Now, for the big deployed systems, inference is plausibly comparable to or larger than training in aggregate. And the new inference-heavy techniques, where you let the model think for a long time before answering, push this further. You're effectively moving compute from the training phase to the deployment phase, and you get capability gains that look somewhat like what you'd get from a larger training run.

One thing I find interesting is that this changes the economics of who can compete. Training a frontier model is a massive one-off investment that only a handful of actors can make. But inference scaling is more incremental. You can buy more capability on the margin by spending more per query, and that's accessible to a much wider set of users and developers. It also means the hardware demand is more continuous, rather than being driven by these lumpy training runs.

So the short answer is that I expect inference to take up an increasing share of total AI compute over time, both because deployment is growing and because we're finding that spending compute at inference time is a genuinely effective way to get more performance. But I'd also caution that these two aren't fully independent. The best inference-time techniques tend to work better on models that have been trained with more compute, so I don't think we're going to see a world where training stops scaling and everything goes to inference. It's more that both grow, and the ratio shifts somewhat toward inference.

r001.rationale: The response says the allocation depends on expected usage and describes a training–inference trade-off, but it does not say the ratio depends on the slope of the performance trade-off.

r002.rationale: It says inference techniques work better on models trained with more compute, but does not clearly state that increasing model scale unlocks inference techniques that raise the returns to inference compute.

r003.rationale: The response describes training and inference as substitutes, but does not explain that an imbalanced allocation leaves relatively cheap performance gains available by increasing the smaller budget.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that training and inference are linked. If you scale up a model, you generally make it more expensive both to train and to run. But how you should balance those costs depends on how much you expect people to use it.

If you’re going to serve a model billions of times, it can be worth spending more on training to get a smaller model to a given level of capability, because you recover that investment through cheaper inference. If you expect relatively little use, you might prefer a larger model trained on less data, even though each inference is more expensive.

So scaling doesn’t automatically imply a particular balance between training and inference spending. Demand matters enormously. As deployment grows, inference can account for a very substantial share of total compute, and that changes which models it makes sense to train in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response says the balance depends on expected usage and demand, but does not state that it depends on the slope of the performance trade-off between inference and training compute.

r002.rationale: It discusses scaling making training and inference more expensive, but does not suggest that larger models unlock inference techniques that improve returns to inference compute.

r003.rationale: It describes choosing models to trade training costs against inference costs based on usage, but does not explain that an imbalanced budget can leave cheap performance gains available by increasing the smaller budget.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key point is that training and inference are linked. Spending more on training can give you a more capable model, but if that model is larger, it will generally also cost more to run. So the right balance depends heavily on how much you expect to use it.

If you’re going to serve billions of queries, it can make sense to spend more upfront on training to make inference cheaper—for example, by training a smaller model for longer. If you expect relatively little use, you might prefer to save on training and accept a higher cost per query.

So scaling doesn’t necessarily push that balance in one direction. As deployment grows, inference can become the dominant cost, and that changes which model sizes and training budgets are economically attractive.

r001.rationale: The response says the balance depends on expected usage, but does not relate the spending ratio to the slope of the performance trade-off between inference and training compute.

r002.rationale: It discusses model size and inference costs, but does not suggest that scaling unlocks inference techniques with higher returns to inference compute.

r003.rationale: It does not explain that an imbalanced allocation leaves relatively cheap performance gains available by increasing the smaller budget.
